I didn't go with the custom MemoryManager trick. For one I would probably have a difficult time figuring out how to do it correctly, and for two because it still feels a bit unnecessary to me. `MemoryMarshal` is an "I know what I am doing" type, and even if we did do it, it would not address the pinning possibility.

Should we doc that the returned `ROM<byte>` has an independent lifetime from the underlying certificate? `ROM<byte>` is supposed to be an abstraction, but we're returning a property whose correct usage relies on the buffer having an independent lifetime, and people will absolutely depend on this behavior. Might be worthwhile to formalize this expectation in docs.

@GrabYourPitchforks 

> Should we doc that the returned `ROM<byte>` has an independent lifetime from the underlying certificate? 

What would documentation like that look like? I... think... given the API shape it's a reasonable expectation (otherwise it'd be a `CopyRawDataTo(..)` or something like that.

Would codifying in a test be more reasonable, or is that not strong enough? (I'm starting to think the test should exist regardless... let me add that).

> Would codifying in a test be more reasonable, or is that not strong enough?

That's probably good enough honestly. Get the `ROM<byte>`, dispose the cert, then validate the buffer you previously got is still filled with delicious X.509 goodness.

issue_context.title: [API Proposal]: X509Certificate2.RawDataMemory
issue_context.body:
### Background and motivation

The `X509Certificate2` class has a property called `RawData` which returns the raw data of the X.509 certificate object in DER form.

This property however allocates every time it is accessed to return a clone to the caller.

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/98ca2ffa27ed23d106e7131bac8cb17a46b905d3/src/libraries/System.Security.Cryptography.X509Certificates/src/System/Security/Cryptography/X509Certificates/X509Certificate2.cs#L315-L326

This means code written like:

```C#
Encode(cert.RawData, cert.RawData.Length)
```

or anything else that accesses `RawData` multiple times is going to allocate a several hundred bytes each time the property is accessed. Removing the defensive copy is likely a breaking change.

It would be good if we exposed a way to get the `RawData` without returning a defensive copy every time. In order to do this, the return type must not expose a way of mutating (assuming safe APIs are being used).

### API Proposal

```diff
namespace System.Security.Cryptography.X509Certificates {
    public class X509Certificate2 : X509Certificate {
+       public ReadOnlyMemory<byte> RawDataMemory { get; }
    }
}
```

### API Usage

```C#
ReadOnlyMemory<byte> certData = cert.RawDataMemory;

// or for those that need a span
ReadOnlySpan<byte> certData = cert.RawDataMemory.Span;
```

### Alternatives

I'm not tied to the idea of returning a `ReadOnlyMemory<byte>`. If something else makes more sense, that's fine too.

### Risks

Small risk would be someone using unsafe APIs or `fixed` to coerce the `ReadOnlyMemory<byte>` in to something writable, but I think that is acceptable.

Author: vcsjones
Assignees: -
Labels: `api-suggestion`, `area-System.Security`
Milestone: -

> If something else makes more sense like `ReadOnlyMemory<byte>` that's fine too.

@stephentoub Do you have thoughts here?  It seems analagous to the Capture.MatchSpan property... ReadOnlyMemory is sort of a stronger type than ReadOnlySpan (in the sense of "return the strongest you can, accept the weakest you need").  Should we be returning ReadOnlyMemory from these properties instead of ReadOnlySpan?  (Yeah, memory carries different, not necessarily fewer, problems...)
How much do you care about the underlying byte[] becoming mutable?

> How much do you care about the underlying byte[] becoming mutable?

I'm not sure I understand, but hopefully this answers, I would expect that the underlying `byte[]` should not be mutable with safe APIs. (That excludes APIs that are already deemed unsafe like `Unsafe.As`, `MemoryMarshal`, etc).

If it matters, `ReadOnlySpan<byte>` seems like it would be preferable to me to avoid doing `memory.Span` since the use-case (for me) that brought this on has span-accepting API surface.

>> How much do you care about the underlying byte[] becoming mutable?

> I'm not sure I understand, but hopefully this answers, I would expect that the underlying byte[] should not be mutable with safe APIs. (That excludes APIs that are already deemed unsafe like Unsafe.As, MemoryMarshal, etc).

With `ReadOnlyMemory<byte>`, the underlying array is directly accessible via `MemoryMarshal.TryGetArray`.  With `ReadOnlySpan<byte>`, you can't get access to the the thing typed as `byte[]` (you could use `Unsafe.AsRef` on `memory.Span.GetPinnableReference` to get a `ref byte`).

> With `ReadOnlyMemory<byte>`, the underlying array is directly accessible via `MemoryMarshal.TryGetArray`. With `ReadOnlySpan<byte>`,

I think that is okay... if someone really wanted to they could reflect on the class today and modify the underlying array. Even with `ReadOnlySpan<byte>` someone could just `fixed` it and write to it. Since `MemoryMarshal` seems to be treated similarly as C# `unsafe`, I don't see them as massively different (maybe that is a naive way of thinking). But modifying it does not have a real use case at all.

I threw `ReadOnlyMemory<byte>` out there but, from an API design perspective, why would returning that be better?

>  from an API design perspective, why would returning that be better?

Consider `public AsnReader(ReadOnlyMemory<byte> data, AsnEncodingRules ruleSet, AsnReaderOptions options = default)`.  If the property returns a ReadOnlySpan you have to copy it to an array, or do dirty tricks like making a MemoryManager that tracks a pinned span for an "I promise I'll be careful" operation.  If the property returns a ReadOnlyMemory then you can still use `.Span` to get a Span, and you can use AsnReader, or Async methods, or whatever.  (e.g. `stream.WriteAsync(cert.RawDataBuffer)`).

So ReadOnlyMemory as a return provides more breadth of use.

> With ReadOnlyMemory<byte>, the underlying array is directly accessible via MemoryMarshal.TryGetArray.

We could put a utility MemoryManager in Common that wraps an array and just returns false from TryGetArray if we wanted to defend against this and be closer to immutable.  I do feel that it's potentially more abused than using unsafe, but not significantly so.  If someone's being malicious they'd use unsafe/Unsafe, so a custom MemoryManager would only stop accidental ReadOnlyMemory->TryGetArray for some compat reason followed by "ooh, I have an array (segment) here...".

As a general pattern, probably not worth it, as a thing in a Security namespace, perhaps worth it.  But, either way, it /could/ be done.
Okay, all that makes sense. I updated the proposal to use a `ReadOnlyMemory<byte>`.
